Our Approach to Seed Selection

We begin with the grower’s requirements: the crop, the cultivation system, the location and the planting window. We then match these against the technical information available for each variety, including growth habit and resistance codes. Where performance depends on local conditions, we say so. Our role is to make selection clearer, so that you can request the seeds you need with confidence.

Understanding resistance codes

HR (high resistance) means a variety strongly restricts the development of the named pest or disease under normal pressure. IR (intermediate resistance) means it restricts development, but may show more symptoms than a high-resistance variety, especially under heavy pressure. Resistance is not immunity. Performance, yield and disease pressure vary with local conditions, growing system and crop management.

CodeDisease or pestType
Immunity

The plant is not attacked or infected by a given pest or pathogen.

Resistance

The variety limits the growth of a given pest or pathogen, or the damage it causes, compared with susceptible varieties in the same conditions. Under heavy pressure some symptoms can still appear.

High resistance (HR)

Strongly limits the pest or pathogen under normal pressure, compared with susceptible varieties.

Intermediate resistance (IR)

Limits the pest or pathogen, but can show more symptoms or damage than a highly resistant variety.

Definitions follow the International Seed Federation (ISF). Resistance does not cover new strains or races of a pathogen.

What we evaluate

Solar-integrated greenhouses and water-saving concepts

Energy and water are the two largest running needs of protected cultivation. We evaluate greenhouse concepts that use sunlight on the roof, and approaches that save and reuse water on site. What is achievable depends on the site, the crop, the climate and how a system is operated, and is confirmed project by project.

Solar on the roof

A photovoltaic roof can generate electricity from sunlight, while the structure shapes the light for the crop below. Output and crop results depend on the design and the site, and are assessed for each project.

Water-saving concepts

We look at ways to collect, filter and reuse water on site. What can be achieved is assessed for each project.

Modular installation

Standard modules are designed for quicker installation. Installation time and site restoration are agreed project by project.

How a project develops

Every project is different, so scope and sequence are set individually. In general, the work moves through five stages.

  1. 1

    Understand

    We learn about your crop, site, objectives and timing.

  2. 2

    Assess

    We review the site, crop and technology options against your requirements.

  3. 3

    Shape the concept

  4. 4

    Propose

  5. 5

    Coordinate

    We coordinate the agreed next steps with you and the parties involved.

To begin, it helps to know

  • The crop or crops you plan to grow.
  • The project location.
  • Approximate site area, and whether the site is new or existing.
  • Your objectives and expected timing.
  • Any drawings or site information you already have (optional).

A short description is enough to start a conversation.

Common questions

What information do I need to get started?

Your crop, location, approximate site area, whether the site is new or existing, and your timing and objectives. A short description is enough to begin.

Can you give a fixed price at the first stage?

Costs depend on project scope and site conditions, so a proposal follows an initial technical review rather than preceding it.

Do you guarantee yields or energy output?

No. Outcomes depend on the site, crop, climate and how the system is operated. We assess options against your requirements and state our assumptions clearly.

Are regulatory approvals included?

Approvals are specific to each project. Responsibilities for them are set out in the proposal for that project.

Can I discuss seeds and greenhouse technology together?

Yes. Our three divisions can be discussed in a single enquiry.

Why it matters in the Gulf

Growing indoors in a hot, dry climate

The Gulf has strong sun, high summer heat, limited fresh water and little farmland. The UAE depends on imports for much of its food. Growing fresh produce close to where it is eaten is therefore of real interest.

Shelter from the heat

A sealed, insulated room keeps crops away from outdoor summer heat. Cooling is part of the design.

Water kept in a loop

Closed-loop irrigation reuses water instead of letting it drain away.

More crop, less ground

Racks stack crops upward, so more growing area fits on a small footprint.

Fresh and close to the table

Produce can be grown near kitchens and shops, and harvested to order.

Indoor farming uses electricity for lights and cooling, so each project is assessed for its own site.

Food security is on the national agenda

The UAE National Food Security Strategy 2051 promotes resilient farming that raises productivity, and the Ziraai programme promotes hydroponics.

Smart growing

Fresh crops, grown close to where they are eaten

Controlled light, water and climate let a small room grow greens, herbs and flowers all year round.

  • Year-round growing
  • Soil-free hydroponics

The technology

How a vertical farm works

A vertical farm combines six technologies. Together they let crops grow in stacked layers, indoors, under control.

Hydroponics

Plants grow with their roots in water that carries dissolved nutrients, with no soil.

Aeroponics

Roots hang in the air and are misted with nutrient solution. It is often used in towers.

LED lighting

Efficient LEDs give plants the light they need, set by schedule, intensity and colour.

Climate control

Cooling, dehumidifying and airflow hold temperature and humidity steady.

CO₂ enrichment

In a sealed room, carbon dioxide can be added in small, controlled amounts to support growth.

Automation

Sensors and a controller run irrigation, lighting and climate, and report to an app.

Around the world

How Japan and other countries do it

Vertical and container farming is already part of the food system in several countries. These examples show what others are doing. They are not claims about any MAD OCEANCONNECT project.

Japan

Plant factories
  • Japan has about 200 plant factories that grow lettuce under artificial light, most of them small.
  • An ageing farm workforce is one reason for automation. One report put the average farmer’s age at 67.
  • Large plants can be nearly fully automated, with people mainly at the end of the line.
  • Lettuce is the main crop, and tomatoes and strawberries are also grown under artificial light. Lighting uses more energy than sun-based farming.
  • Spread’s Techno Farm Keihanna is an automated lettuce plant that has been reported at about 30,000 heads a day.
  • Mirai built its own plant factories, including one in Miyagi that was reported at 10,000 heads a day.
What these examples share

Climate-controlled rooms, hydroponic water loops, LED light and software control. Results differ by crop, site and electricity cost.

Singapore

A city with little land
  • Singapore imports nearly 90% of its food and farms only about 1% of its land.
  • Its 30 by 30 goal aims to produce 30% of nutritional needs locally by 2030.
  • Rooftop and indoor farms grow greens hydroponically in climate-controlled rooms.
  • Sky Greens opened in 2012 as an early commercial vertical farm.

United States

Early movers and hard lessons
  • Early commercial vertical farms opened in 2014, such as Green Spirit Farms in Pennsylvania, with racks six high.
  • Several operators now run more than one indoor farm.
  • Not every venture has lasted. Some early farms closed, so careful planning matters.
  • Square Roots began in a Brooklyn parking lot in 2016 and grows in modular shipping-container farms.
  • Farm.One grows salad greens, herbs, edible flowers and microgreens for chefs in New York.
  • Gotham Greens opened a rooftop greenhouse in Brooklyn in 2013 on top of a supermarket. It is a greenhouse, not a container.

Netherlands

Research and glasshouse know-how
  • Wageningen University and Research built a test facility with four airtight growing cells.
  • LED lighting in the cells can be adjusted in level and colour to study how plants respond.
  • Systems measure photosynthesis, water and nutrient uptake, and the full energy balance.
  • Tests include growing leafy vegetables in several layers.

UAE and the Gulf

Dubai and beyond
  • Bustanica, near Dubai, is run by Emirates Crop One and opened in July 2022 with 330,000 sq ft of hydroponic growing space.
  • It grows leafy greens, with plans for other vegetables and fruit.
  • Its operators report using about 95% less water than conventional farming.
  • The Ziraai programme promotes hydroponics on UAE farms.
  • Badia Farms in Dubai was reported as the first commercial vertical farm in the GCC, growing microgreens under LED light.
  • In Qatar, the Qur’anic Botanic Garden and the University of Arizona are developing a shipping-container vertical farming model.
  • Agrico and iFarm announced a vertical-farm trial at Al Khor, Qatar.

System types

Four ways to grow vertically

The same ideas come in different sizes. The right system depends on your space, your crop and how much you want to grow.

Shelf or rack systems

Stacked shelves with LED strips above each layer. This is the most common layout for leafy greens, herbs and microgreens.

Best for: Rooms, kitchens and containers.

Tower systems

Vertical columns where plants grow around the tower, fed by dripping or misting. Often used for strawberries and leafy greens.

Best for: Small footprints and display growing.

Container farms

A complete growing room in a 40-foot container, with climate, water and lighting built in.

Best for: Businesses that want a ready-made growing room.

Home units

A compact cabinet for a kitchen or balcony room, with built-in lights and a glass door. Home units are in development.

Best for: Families and small kitchens.

Renders show the idea of each system and are not to scale. Our focus is container systems, starting with 40-foot containers.

Comparison

Container farm, greenhouse or open field

Each way of growing has its place. This is a general, qualitative comparison to help you see where a container fits.

Topic
Container farm
Greenhouse
Open field
ClimateFully controlled in a sealed roomPartly controlled with vents, shading and coolingNone. Crops follow the weather
WaterRecirculated in a closed loopCan be recirculated, depending on the systemDepends on irrigation, with more loss to soil and air
Land neededVery small footprintModerateLargest
Growing seasonYear-roundExtended seasonSeasonal
Energy useHighest, mainly lighting and coolingModerate, mainly cooling and fansLowest
Weather and pest exposureLow, with strict hygieneReducedFully exposed
Crop rangeGreens, herbs, microgreens, flowers and some fruitWide, including tall fruiting cropsWidest, including field crops
Equipment costHighest per square metre of growing areaModerateLowest
Best forFresh produce near the customer, year-roundFruiting vegetables and flowers at scaleStaple and large-area crops

A general comparison only. Real results depend on the crop, the site and how the system is run.

Questions and answers

Is the container energy-independent?

No. Solar panels can assist a container with part of its electricity, subject to feasibility for the site, but they do not replace a power connection. We make no claim of energy independence.

Are the pilot containers operating?

Not yet. Our specialty-mushroom pilot is planned, with two intended locations, subject to technical and commercial assessment. We will report results only once they have been measured.

Do you guarantee yield, savings or returns?

No. Outcomes depend on the site, the crop and how a system is run. The calculators on this site are arithmetic on figures you enter, not forecasts.

Can I visit a working container?

Demonstration visits are subject to confirmation. Partner-operated sites are shown only with the owner’s written permission, and our own pilot can be visited once it is operating.

Which crops can a container grow?

Mushrooms are the crop of our planned pilot. Leafy greens, herbs, microgreens and specialty greens can be assessed for a project.

What we do

We build the container, the control system and the connection

Container farming brings a growing room to any site. Our work covers the whole system, so that one team is responsible for how it is built, how it runs and how you manage it.

Custom container builds

We design and build growing containers around your crop, your site and your use, with racks, lighting, water and climate equipment fitted.

Automated control

Climate, irrigation and lighting are managed by a control system, so the growing room holds the conditions each crop needs.

Solar power options

Solar panels can go on the roof, sides or end of a container to assist its electricity supply, subject to feasibility for each site.

Remote operation

Sensors report to an app, and you can see the container and manage it from wherever you are.

Inside the container

Five zones, from the door to the technical room

A 40-foot container is arranged along its length. You enter through an airlock, grow in two racked zones either side of a central aisle, and the equipment sits in its own technical room.

  1. Entry and airlockSanitation and access control at the door.
  2. Growing zone 1Vertical racking, suited to leafy greens and herbs.
  3. Central aisleLighting, irrigation and sensors run along the aisle.
  4. Growing zone 2Vertical racking, suited to mushrooms and specialty crops.
  5. Technical roomWater tanks, pumps, climate control and electrical equipment.

Planning tools

Vertical Farming Scenario Planner

Three planning calculators for vertical farming and container projects: solar saving, cultivation and investment. Enter your own figures, or load an illustrative example. Results are arithmetic on those figures, not a forecast, a quote or a promise.

Nothing is pre-filled. Estimates only, not a quotation.

You can load an illustrative example. Every example figure is marked as an assumption, and a figure you change is marked as your own. The examples are not measured, quoted or verified data.

Solar saving

Estimate what a solar system could save on your grid electricity bill. Enter your own figures, or load the illustrative example.

Scenario
The solar system
Use a figure from your own solar design.
Your electricity
Solar output that is not used on site is not valued here.
Use the tariff on your own bill.
Costs
Scenarios

Each scenario changes your figures by the percentages below. You can edit them.

Output change (%)Tariff change (%)Cost change (%)
Conservative
Base
Optimistic
How this is calculated
  • Solar output = for each side, kWp × yearly output per kWp, added together.
  • Solar used on site = the smaller of (output × share used on site) and your electricity use.
  • Gross grid savings = solar used on site × grid tariff.
  • Net grid savings = gross grid savings − service and maintenance.
  • Coverage = solar used on site ÷ electricity use.
  • Simple payback = installation cost ÷ net grid savings.

The calculator does not include financing, tariff changes over time, battery storage, panel ageing or export income. It does not use market data and does not promise any saving. Your figures stay in your browser.

Cultivation

Estimate the yearly economics of one growing container. Enter your own figures, or load the illustrative example. Example figures are assumptions, not measured results.

Scenario
Production and sales
Use your own expected harvest. No yield is promised on this site.
Use your own expected price.
Costs per cycle and per kg sold
Yearly running costs (AED)
Optional. Use the result of the solar tab or your own figure.
Scenarios

Each scenario changes your figures by the percentages below. You can edit them.

Harvest change (%)Price change (%)Cost change (%)
Conservative
Base
Optimistic
How this is calculated
  • Harvest per year = containers × cycles × harvest per cycle.
  • Saleable harvest = harvest per year × saleable share.
  • Revenue = saleable harvest × selling price.
  • Total cost = substrate × cycles × containers + yearly running costs (electricity less any solar saving) + (packing + transport) × saleable harvest.
  • Margin = operating surplus ÷ revenue.
  • Cost per kg = total cost ÷ harvest per year.
  • Operating surplus = revenue − total cost.
  • Break-even price = total cost ÷ saleable harvest.

The calculator does not include financing, taxes, equipment depreciation or the timing of sales. It does not use market data and does not predict a yield or a price. Your figures stay in your browser.

Investment

Compare simple investment arithmetic across three scenarios. Enter your own figures, or load the illustrative example.

Scenario
Investment (AED)
Operating result
The yearly cash you expect after running costs.
Leave empty to skip the net present value.
Scenarios

Each scenario changes your figures by the percentages below. You can edit them.

Cash flow change (%)CAPEX change (%)Working capital change (%)
Conservative
Base
Optimistic
How this is calculated
  • CAPEX = container and fit-out + site preparation + solar installation.
  • Total investment = CAPEX + reserve + working capital.
  • Simple annual ROI = annual operating cash flow ÷ total investment.
  • Simple payback = total investment ÷ annual operating cash flow.
  • Net position over the horizon = annual operating cash flow × years − total investment.
  • Net present value is shown only if a discount rate is entered.

The calculator is simple arithmetic. It does not include financing, taxes, depreciation or resale value, does not calculate an internal rate of return, and does not promise any return. Your figures stay in your browser.

In development

Research, Knowledge Exchange & Innovation

MAD OCEANCONNECT aims to support closer connections between Southern European agricultural expertise and the UAE. We are exploring opportunities for university and institutional collaboration in seed suitability, protected cultivation, crop adaptation and agricultural technology transfer. These initiatives are in development and will be communicated as formal projects are established.

  • Seed suitability
  • Protected cultivation
  • Crop adaptation and technology transfer
  • Vertical and container farming

Where we see opportunity

Seed suitability

Understanding how varieties perform under UAE conditions, and how that information can inform selection.

Protected cultivation

Exploring approaches to greenhouse production suited to regional climate, light, water and energy use.

Crop adaptation and technology transfer

Considering how knowledge and technology developed elsewhere can be evaluated for local conditions.

New area of interest

Vertical and container farming

Vertical and container farming grows crops in stacked layers inside a controlled, enclosed space, such as a converted shipping container. In a hot, dry climate such as the UAE, growing indoors is an area we are exploring, because climate, water and light can be managed closely inside the space.

We are exploring which crops suit these systems and how they could be evaluated under local conditions. Our intention is to work with universities and institutions on this.

About Us

MAD OCEANCONNECT is a UAE-based agricultural business focused primarily on professional seeds and seed solutions. We connect commercial growers and agricultural projects with seed varieties selected according to crop requirements, growing systems and local conditions.

Our Consulting division delivers specialist agricultural consulting and greenhouse technology solutions, including project design, installation and agronomic guidance. Our Vertical Farming division is developing indoor and container-based cultivation.

Technology-led from the start

Always looking for the best and newest technology

MAD OCEANCONNECT is a UAE-based company with a strong focus on technology. We are always looking for better seed genetics, newer growing systems and smarter tools that help growers in the Gulf region work more efficiently.

We follow developments in protected cultivation, agrivoltaic greenhouses, indoor and container farming, climate and water control, and farm management software. We also study what is being done in leading agricultural countries.

When a technology looks promising, we assess it against local conditions before we bring it to our customers. We work with specialist breeders and technology providers, so that growers can use modern solutions without having to build the expertise alone.

Always searching

We look for the newest seed varieties and growing technology.

Assessed for the Gulf

New ideas are checked against heat, water and market conditions here.

Connected to experts

We work with breeders, engineers and agronomists in Europe and the Gulf.

Built to grow

Systems range from a home unit to a multi-container farm.

Greenhouse Profit Calculator

A free tool for a first planning estimate. Enter your own figures for area, yield, price and costs. Nothing is pre-filled, and the result is a planning estimate, not a forecast or guarantee.

The project
The total investment in structure and equipment.
Production and sales
Share of the harvest that cannot be sold.
Use your own expected price.
Annual operating costs (AED)
Scenarios

Each scenario changes your base figures by the percentages below. You can edit them.

Yield change (%)Price change (%)Cost change (%)
Conservative
Base
Optimistic

Example values only, not a forecast. Replace them with your own figures.

How this is calculated
  • Marketable produce = area × gross yield per m² × (1 − wastage).
  • Revenue = marketable produce × price per kg.
  • Operating profit = revenue − annual operating costs.
  • Margin = operating profit ÷ revenue.
  • Break-even price = annual operating costs ÷ marketable produce.
  • Simple payback = capital cost ÷ annual operating profit. It is shown as not reached when profit is zero or negative.
  • The scenarios apply your percentage changes to yield, price and operating costs.

The calculator does not include financing, taxes, depreciation, seasonal variation or the timing of cash flows. It does not use market data. Your figures stay in your browser.

Privacy Notice

This notice explains how MAD OCEANCONNECT uses the details you send through this website.

What we collect

When you submit an enquiry, we receive the details you enter in the form, such as your name, company, email address, phone number, location and the information about your crop or project.

Why we use it

We use these details only to respond to your enquiry, to prepare a quotation or project proposal, and to follow up on that enquiry. We do this with your consent, which you give by ticking the consent box on the form.

Who can see it

Your enquiry is read by the MAD OCEANCONNECT team responsible for your request. We do not sell your details or share them for marketing.

How long we keep it

We keep enquiry details only for as long as they are needed to handle your request and any business relationship that follows, and then delete them.

Your choices

You can ask to see, correct or delete the details we hold about you, or withdraw your consent, by contacting our office on +971 50 877 2747.

Stored in your browser

This website does not use analytics or advertising cookies. It keeps your Quote List, saved lists, calculator scenarios, language and display settings in your own browser so that they are still there when you return. You can clear them at any time in your browser settings.
